patient_name: OET role-play — older man with a venous leg ulcer who keeps taking off his compression bandage
chief_complaint: On a home visit, find out why a patient keeps removing his compression bandage, explain why compression heals venous leg ulcers, and agree a plan to keep it on

team_brief.title: Venous leg ulcer: a patient who takes his compression bandage off at night
team_brief.patient: Mr Kenneth Walsh, 79-year-old retired postman with a venous leg ulcer on his left inner ankle for five months
team_brief.location: Mr Walsh's home; you are the community nurse on a routine home visit to change his dressing and compression bandage
team_brief.situation: Mr Walsh has a compression bandage applied twice a week. For the second time this week you find it removed and his leg swollen. The ulcer has not got smaller in the last month.
background: The ulcer is caused by poor circulation in the leg veins. A circulation check (Doppler assessment) last month showed the arteries in his legs are healthy enough for full compression, and compression bandaging was started then.
He lives alone, walks with a stick, and spends most of the day in an armchair with his feet on the floor.
He goes to a social club every Thursday and likes to wear his own shoes there, but his usual left shoe does not fit over the bandage.
current_status: Left lower leg is swollen; the ulcer is about the size of a large coin, with no signs of spreading infection.
He says the bandage 'throbs' at night and he takes it off at bedtime; he took simple pain relief only once this week.
key_data: In a venous leg ulcer, the valves in the leg veins do not work well, so blood and fluid collect in the lower leg; the pressure and swelling stop the skin healing.

Compression squeezes the leg to help the blood flow back up towards the heart, which reduces swelling and helps the ulcer heal. Most venous ulcers heal with consistent compression, but healing slows when it is taken off.
Discomfort usually eases as the swelling goes down, often within the first couple of weeks; pain relief as prescribed, taken before bed, and raising the legs above hip level when resting can help.
Walking and moving the ankle up and down often during the day work the calf muscle, which pumps blood back up the leg; sitting for long periods with the feet down makes the swelling worse.

Warning signs: toes that become cold, blue or pale, numbness or pins and needles, or severe pain. If these happen, he should unwind and remove the bandage and contact the nursing team straight away (or the out-of-hours service).
Footwear: a larger, wide-fitting shoe or a special bandage shoe can be worn over the bandage; the team can advise on or supply one.
If the bandage is not tolerated, the team can review other compression options (for example, a lighter system or a compression wrap) — it should not simply be stopped.
treatments: Already done: Doppler circulation check; twice-weekly dressing and compression bandaging.
Pending: review of compression options if he still cannot tolerate the bandage; review by the GP of his pain relief if needed.
team_brief.your_request: Find out why Mr Walsh is removing the bandage, explain why compression matters, and agree a plan that helps him keep it on.
must_include: Find out why Mr Walsh is removing the bandage, without judging him.
Explain in simple terms how compression helps a venous leg ulcer to heal.
Advise him on ways to reduce discomfort (pain relief before bed, raising his legs, gentle walking and ankle exercises).
Explain the warning signs that mean the bandage is too tight and what to do.
Persuade him to keep the bandage on and agree a plan, including a solution for wearing shoes to his club.

kickoff_text: Morning, nurse. Before you say anything — yes, I took it off again. It was throbbing all night. It's too tight, that thing.
persona_override: You are Kenneth Walsh, a 79-year-old retired postman with a leg ulcer on your left ankle. You are friendly, independent and a bit stubborn, and you do not like fuss. Your specific belief: the bandage is so tight that it 'stops the blood getting to the leg', so you think it is actually making the ulcer worse, and it throbs at night so you cannot sleep. Underneath, you are also annoyed that you cannot get your good shoe on for your Thursday social club, and you are starting to lose hope that the ulcer will ever heal. Ground truth: the ulcer has been there five months; the bandage was started about a month ago and is changed twice a week; you take it off at bedtime about three nights a week; the throbbing is worst in the first hour in bed, and hanging your leg out of bed does not particularly help; your toes have never gone numb, cold or blue; you took paracetamol only once this week because you 'don't like taking tablets'; you sit in your armchair most of the day with your feet on the floor; you walk with a stick to the shop. You did not know the ulcer is caused by the veins, not the arteries, or that the circulation test last month was to check the bandage was safe. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses words like 'venous insufficiency', 'oedema', 'Doppler', 'ABPI', 'multilayer compression' or 'elevation' without explaining them, ask what they mean. If the nurse tells you off or just says you must keep it on without asking why you take it off, get grumpy: 'It's my leg. You try sleeping in it.' If the nurse does not deal with your belief that the bandage cuts off the blood, repeat it more anxiously: 'But surely squeezing it that tight stops the blood getting to the sore?' If the nurse explains that the problem is blood not getting back out of the leg, and that the circulation test showed the bandage is safe for you, soften gradually and ask 'So why does it throb, then?' Accept pain relief before bed and raising your legs, but only agree to keep the bandage on overnight if the nurse also tells you what warning signs mean you should take it off. Only mention that your good shoe will not go on over the bandage if the nurse asks what else bothers you about it or about your week. If the nurse offers a solution for your shoe (for example, a larger shoe or special bandage shoe for now), become more cooperative. If the nurse checks understanding, repeat the plan back but forget one part (for example, raising your legs). Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: agree to try keeping the bandage on until the next visit and thank the nurse.
learning_objectives: find out why the patient removes the compression bandage without judging him
explain how compression helps blood flow back from the leg and heals the ulcer
advise pain relief before bed, raising the legs and ankle exercises
explain warning signs such as cold, blue or numb toes and what to do
agree a plan and a solution for wearing shoes to his club
check understanding by asking him to repeat the plan
suggested_questions: Thanks for being honest with me. Can you tell me what happens at night that makes you take it off?
The problem with your leg isn't blood getting in — it's blood and fluid not getting back out. The bandage gently squeezes the leg to push that fluid back up, and that's what lets the sore heal.
The throbbing usually settles as the swelling goes down. Taking your pain relief about half an hour before bed and putting your feet up in the evening can really help.
If your toes ever go cold, blue or numb, or the pain becomes severe, take the bandage off and ring us straight away. Otherwise, could we try keeping it on until my next visit?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Promoting concordance with compression therapy for a venous leg ulcer
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries on venous leg ulcers and NHS leg ulcer information; the compression system, assessment and review schedule follow local tissue viability policy
core_concepts: Compression therapy is the main treatment for venous leg ulcers; inconsistent use is a leading reason ulcers fail to heal.
Arterial assessment (for example, Doppler) before full compression is essential, because compression can harm a leg with poor arterial supply.
Discomfort, poor sleep, footwear problems and misunderstanding of how compression works are common reasons patients remove bandages.
diagnostic_clues: Swelling on arrival and a non-shrinking ulcer suggest compression is not being kept on.
Throbbing that eases with time and no numbness or colour change points to discomfort from swelling rather than arterial compromise, but warning signs must still be taught.
Pain that is worse in bed or with the legs raised and eased by hanging the leg down can suggest arterial disease; even after a recent satisfactory Doppler, it needs prompt reassessment.
common_misconceptions: A tight bandage cuts off the blood supply in a venous ulcer.
Compression can be taken off at night without affecting healing.
An ulcer that has not healed in months will never heal.
dangerous_errors: Telling the patient to ignore numbness, colour change or severe pain under a bandage.
Blaming or lecturing the patient, which reduces concordance further.
Agreeing that compression can simply be stopped rather than arranging a review of alternatives.
management_principles: Explore the patient's reasons and beliefs before explaining.
Explain the mechanism of compression in lay terms and address symptom control (analgesia, elevation, movement).
Teach warning signs, agree a realistic plan including practical fixes such as footwear, and arrange review of the compression system if needed.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Compression systems, pressure levels and arterial assessment thresholds (for example, ABPI values) vary between products and local tissue viability policy.
Advice on whether a patient should remove a bandage themselves if warning signs appear, and whom to contact out of hours, follows local community nursing policy.
Analgesia choice and dose follow the prescription; signs of infection, sudden pain, or suspected arterial disease need prompt clinical review.
